e.etymology: In American use a short form of Kamila, Kamryn and similar names, a K spelling of Cami. Kami is also a Persian pet form of Kamran and the Japanese word for a god or spirit.

assoc.t: kami, the gods and spirits of Japanese Shinto

e.etymology: A spelling of Callie, a pet form of Caroline, Calista and other Cal- names. It is also a Greek short form of Kalliope, from kallos, 'beauty'.
Two names share this spelling: Arabic Kamil, 'perfect, complete', and the Polish, Czech and Slovak form of Latin Camillus, a Roman family name of unknown, probably Etruscan, origin.
The Hawaiian word for angel, borrowed from English. A separate Anela, a form of Angela, is used in Bosnia and Croatia; both go back to Greek angelos, 'messenger'.
From the surname Quade or Quaid, shortened from Irish McQuade (Mac Uaid), 'son of Wat', a medieval pet form of Walter.
A respelling of Silas, the New Testament companion of Paul, whose name is a Greek short form of Silvanus, from Latin silva, 'forest'.

assoc.t: Sylus, love interest in the game Love and Deepspace

e.etymology: From the English word for a light wind, borrowed in the 16th century from Spanish or Portuguese briza. Breeze is also a surname, a variant of Breese or from Welsh ap Rhys, 'son of Rhys'.
From Sanskrit shloka, the two-line verse form of the Hindu epics and scriptures. The word also means praise or renown.
e.note: English speakers may say it like schlock, slang for cheap or shoddy goods.

e.etymology: From Arabic ahsan, 'best' or 'most beautiful', the superlative of hasan, 'good, handsome'. It is especially common in Pakistan and Bangladesh.
The Ancient Greek word for truth, literally 'not hidden', and the name of the Greek spirit of truthfulness. English has used the form Alethea since the 17th century.
A recent American name close in sound to Alani and Leilani. Aloni is also a Hebrew name and surname from alon, 'oak'.
A spelling of Kylan, a modern American name that extends Kyle with the ending of Dylan and Rylan.
A Spanish phonetic spelling of Jason, common in Colombia, Venezuela and the Dominican Republic. Jason is Greek Iason, linked to iasthai, 'to heal', the hero who led the Argonauts.
From Old Norse Tyr, the one-handed god of war and justice, whose name goes back to a Proto-Germanic word for 'god'. Tuesday is named for his Old English counterpart Tiw.

assoc.t: Tyr, Norse god of war and justice
Tyr in the God of War Ragnarok video game

e.etymology: The English number word, from Italian milione, 'great thousand'. Million is an established men's name in Ethiopia and Eritrea, and American use also follows word names such as Legend and Royal.
From Old English Weland, the master smith of Germanic legend known as Wayland the Smith. As a surname it can also come from places meaning 'land by the road'. Waylon is a later variant.

assoc.t: Wayland the Smith, blacksmith of Germanic legend

e.etymology: A modern American name close to Amari and Imani. Imari is also a port town in Japan that gave its name to Imari porcelain.
From Latin Fabius, the name of a great Roman family, traditionally derived from faba, 'bean'. It is common in Italy, Brazil and Spanish-speaking countries.
namesakes: Fabio Lanzoni (model of romance-novel covers, known simply as Fabio)
e.note: Many Americans picture Fabio, the romance-novel cover model of the 1990s.

e.etymology: A spelling that sits between Linden, the tree, and Lyndon, an English surname and place name from Old English lind, 'lime (linden) tree', and dun, 'hill'.
From Arabic Abd al-Aziz, 'servant of the Mighty One'. Al-Aziz is one of the 99 names of God in Islam. Abdulaziz ibn Saud founded modern Saudi Arabia.
The Arabic form of Gabriel, from Hebrew Gavriel, 'God is my strength'. In Islam Jibril is the angel who brought the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad.
A Welsh surname, from ap Rhys, 'son of Rhys'. Rhys is an old Welsh name usually glossed as 'ardor' or 'enthusiasm'; Price is the more common spelling.

assoc.t: sounds the same as price, what something costs

e.etymology: A recent American name that extends Kai, in step with Makai and Zakai. Nakai is also a Navajo family name and a Japanese surname.
From an Arabic root describing something fine, slender and delicate. It has been a popular girls' name in the Levant and the Gulf since the late 20th century.
A phonetic spelling of Bodhi, the Sanskrit and Pali word for awakening or enlightenment in Buddhism. The same sound is shared by the surname Bodie and by Bode.
A recent name that reads as Millie plus the -ana ending of Liliana and Juliana. It is also seen as a form of Emiliana or Milana.
A spelling of Idris, a prophet named in the Quran and often identified with the Biblical Enoch. Arabic tradition links the name to darasa, 'to study'.
From metztli, the Nahuatl (Aztec) word for the moon and the name of an Aztec moon deity. It is given to girls in Mexico and in Mexican American families.
A modern American name in the pattern of Ciara and Tiara with the De- opening of Deanna and Deja; it is also written De'arra.
A spelling of Valerie, the French form of Latin Valeria, the feminine of the Roman family name Valerius, from valere, 'to be strong, to be well'.
A form of Corinna, from Greek Korinna, a diminutive of kore, 'maiden'. Corinna was a Greek lyric poet, and Ovid gave the name to the woman of his love poems.
A spelling of Lena or Layna said LAY-nuh. Lena is a short form of names ending in -lena, such as Helena and Magdalena.
